docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: The path from the current state to chora 1.0. Version 1.0 is a daily driver with a stable, versioned API (D3).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Each milestone is a minor release: 0.6, 0.7 and so on.
  • Each milestone has a goal, a scope, an estimate and a gate.
  • The gate is a list of checks. A check is a CI job or a step on the reference hardware with a log as evidence (D46).
  • A milestone is done when every check of its gate holds. The next milestone of the core starts only then.
  • Each milestone has a gate issue on GitHub with the checks as a task list. Each ticked check links to its CI run or log. The release of the milestone closes the issue.
  • Two tracks run in parallel to the core: the XP showroom and the voice pipeline.
  • The showroom track has no milestones of its own. Its CI must be green against each release candidate of the core, so every core gate has that check.
  • The voice track has milestones of its own. It never blocks the core.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text:
• The core runs nested and as a login session. It has no long run on real hardware.
  • The scene has five node kinds, 4x4 transforms, cameras, overlay roots, meshes, effects and animations.
  • The API covers scene changes, events, grabs, plugin methods, captures, input injection, grants, programs, assets and output configuration.
  • choractl loads views and serves MCP.
  • chora-tiling and the XP showroom are plugins in this repository.
  • The core crate has 37 unit tests. IPC dispatch, transactions and the tty backend have none. Pixel tests in a headless sway check the behavior.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
The estimates count the lines of Rust that a milestone adds or changes. They also count the hours of agent work and the hours of hands-on work of the user. The calendar time includes the gate. Agent hours include the tests and the review rounds.

The basis is this repository: about 26,000 lines of Rust in 54 hours of calendar time. A rework of existing code costs more than new code. The table uses about 140 to 200 lines per agent hour for 0.6 to 0.9. The milestones 0.10 and 1.0 have hardware work and use about 80 to 125.

The user uses chora as the daily session from milestone 0.10. The gates of 0.10 and 1.0 measure that use, so they set the calendar time.

Milestone Rust lines Agent hours User hours Calendar 0.6 Foundation 2,500 14 to 18 3 1 week 0.7 Identity and processes 3,000 16 to 20 3 1 to 2 weeks 0.8 Agent read model 4,600 23 to 30 3 2 weeks 0.9 Renderer 7,000 40 to 50 6 3 weeks 0.10 Daily driver 2,500 20 to 30 8 plus daily use 3 weeks 1.0 Stable API 1,500 12 to 16 4 plus daily use 5 to 6 weeks Total 21,100 125 to 164 27 15 to 17 weeks

The renderer has the largest risk. A fault on real hardware in 0.10 can add one to two weeks.

docs.title: 0.6: Foundation
docs.text:
Goal: the project works with gates in the GitHub organization chora. Unit tests check the core in process.

Scope:

  • The organization chora with the repositories of D36. The plugins move to repositories of their own. They depend on chora-scene through a git tag of the core.
  • The git flow of D47 in every repository: a protected main, releases from a merge commit and an annotated tag.
  • The release workflow starts from a tag and needs a green CI run of the same commit.
  • A pinned Rust toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml, a job for the minimum Rust version, and container images pinned by digest.
  • The core as a library and a binary (D48). IPC dispatch, the transaction queue, focus and grants run in unit tests with a fake clock.
  • A headless test backend that renders with pixman in process, for pixel tests in Rust.
  • A smoke test in a VM with vkms in CI (D11). chora starts on the tty backend and shows a foot window. A capture shows its pixels.
  • The website repository builds the user documentation. The reference documentation stays with the code of the core.

Gate:

  1. Every repository of D36 exists, and main accepts pull requests only.
  2. A test release v0.6.0-rc.1 comes from a tag on a merge commit. A tag on a commit with red CI starts no release.
  3. cargo test runs at least 40 unit tests of the core crate for IPC, transactions, focus and grants, without a compositor.
  4. One pixel test runs in process on the pixman backend.
  5. The vkms job is green in 10 runs in a row.
  6. chora-tiling and chora-xp build and pass their tests in their own repositories against the tag of the core.
  7. tests/nested.sh, tests/agent.sh and tests/xp.sh are green in CI.
  8. rust-toolchain.toml pins the toolchain, and the job for the minimum Rust version is green.
  9. Every container image in the workflows has a digest.
  10. The website builds from its repository.
  11. The showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: 0.7: Identity and processes
docs.text:
Goal: a client cannot take another name or give itself capabilities, and the core starts no programs.

Scope:

  • One socket directory per client: $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/clients/NAME/ with ipc.sock and a Wayland socket of wp-security-context-v1 (D33, D40). The socket fixes the name and the capabilities of its clients.
  • An admin socket for choractl only. grants.set and the reset work through it alone.
  • choractl clients up creates the sockets from ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml. The emergency reset removes the client sockets.
  • An example Quadlet unit in dist/ for an agent container that mounts its client directory.
  • A versioned hello with the protocol version and the features of both sides (D29).
  • Structured errors: a stable code for each kind of failure, and data with the index of the failed command.
  • The capability input.grab-any allows grabs without Ctrl, Alt or Super (D45).
  • process.spawn, process.wait and plugins.restart leave the core (D42). choractl run starts a program through systemd-run --user with an activation token. systemctl --user restart restarts a plugin. journald keeps the output.
  • surface.created carries the pid and the activation token.

Gate:

  1. A Podman container that mounts only clients/agent/ queries the scene and draws a node. Its grants.set and its hello with another name fail. A CI job checks this.
  2. A Quadlet unit from dist/ connects through its client directory after a restart of chora, without a change to the unit.
  3. A client with input.grab-any grabs F13 and a letter key. A client without it gets the error code for a missing capability.
  4. The core has no code that forks a process except the startup command.
  5. choractl run foot starts foot in its own systemd scope, and the surface.created event of its window carries the activation token.
  6. Each error code of the API has a test that provokes it.
  7. The gate checks of the earlier milestones still hold, and the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: 0.8: Agent read model
docs.text:
Goal: an agent sees what the user sees, it can ask the window manager for changes, and it can label what it shows.

Scope:

  • JSON filters replace the selector strings (D32). They can match focus and visibility.
  • events.subscribe starts with a snapshot of the state, and every event has a sequence number. An unknown event name is an error.
  • Focus in queries, and a focus.changed event.
  • Queries return the screen rectangle of a node on each output. input.inject takes a node and a point inside it.
  • A client that does not own a node can request a change: focus, move, resize or close. The core sends the request to the owner as an event, and the owner decides (D31). chora-tiling handles the requests.
  • Plugin methods carry a description and a JSON schema. choractl mcp makes one tool from each method (D34).
  • choractl mcp uses rmcp, answers requests in parallel and supports cancellation.
  • Text injection types every character of the text, also characters that the current keymap does not have, for example German umlauts on a US layout.
  • A visible indicator while a client injects input, and a binding of the safety layer that revokes the capabilities of all agents (D23).
  • A text node (D18): text with a font family, a size, a color and a maximum width. cosmic-text shapes it and finds fallback fonts. The indicator, plugins and agents use it for labels without a client.

Gate:

  1. An MCP client in CI calls the tools to focus the second terminal and to request a move to the right. chora-tiling performs both, and a capture shows them.
  2. Under a camera with pan and zoom, a click on a node through the MCP tools hits that node in 20 of 20 tries.
  3. wait_events returns while another tool call runs, and a cancelled call ends within 100 ms.
  4. Injected text Grüße äöüß appears unchanged in foot on a US layout.
  5. A subscription that starts during a transaction misses no event and sees no event twice: a test with 1,000 transactions checks the sequence numbers.
  6. The tool list of choractl mcp matches the exported methods of the plugins after each methods.export.
  7. A capture shows the indicator while a client injects input.
  8. A test shows that the revoke binding removes the capabilities of all agents.
  9. A text node shows Grüße 你好 🙂 with fallback fonts, and a pixel test against a reference capture passes.
  10. An MCP client puts a text node under screen:NAME, and a capture shows it.
  11. The gate checks of the earlier milestones still hold, and the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: 0.9: Renderer
docs.text:
Goal: the core renders only what changed, draws the full 4x4 model, and drives plugins with the frame clock (D17, D24).

Scope:

  • A retained scene: each node keeps its world transform, its bounds and its render resources. Integer handles replace string keys inside the renderer.
  • A scene renderer of chora on GLES 3. It draws each node as a quad with its full matrix. Rounded corners, borders and clips come from signed distance fields in the same pass.
  • A layer renders offscreen only for group opacity, effects or an explicit cache. A layer keeps its texture until its subtree changes. Textures have mipmaps, and their resolution follows the size on screen.
  • A redraw state machine per output. Without damage, the output renders nothing and the loop sleeps. A fullscreen surface without effects goes to direct scanout.
  • Frame events with the predicted presentation time for subscribed plugins (D28). Animations run on the same clock. They interpolate translation, rotation and scale apart, run per property, and support springs.
  • Transactions on disjoint surfaces do not wait for each other (D22).
  • Image decode, shader compile and capture encode run on worker threads.
  • The watchdog runs in its own thread with a heartbeat of the main loop (D23).
  • Debug counters for rendered frames and texture allocations, readable through the API.
  • fd passing for images and captures over the IPC socket (D54).
  • A measurement of the plugin round trip at 120 Hz decides on a private Wayland protocol for plugins (D54).

Gate:

  1. A static scene with rounded windows, a clipped group and a blurred panel renders 0 frames in 10 s of idle time. A counter of the core shows it, in CI and on the reference hardware.
  2. On the reference hardware at the refresh rate of the internal panel: four windows with blur and rounded corners and a 300 ms transition. presentation-time shows 99 percent of the frames on time over 60 s.
  3. A node with rotation and no size renders. A camera with zoom 2 keeps text sharp: a pixel test against a reference capture passes.
  4. A size animation of a layer over 2 s allocates no new texture after the first frame. A counter of the texture pool shows it.
  5. A client that delays its commit for 150 ms delays no transaction of another client. A unit test checks it.
  6. A main loop that blocks for 5 s triggers the watchdog. A test with a debug hook checks it.
  7. The wobbly windows, the magic lamp and the cube of the showroom run on frame events. At 60 Hz and at 120 Hz in CI, 99 percent of their frames are on time over 30 s.
  8. The decision on the plugin protocol is in the decision log, with the measurement.
  9. The gate checks of the earlier milestones still hold, and the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: 0.10: Daily driver
docs.text:
Goal: the user works in chora every day on the reference hardware, and installs it from a package repository.

Scope:

  • Packages through COPR with Packit and subpackages per plugin, and PKGBUILDs in the AUR (D49). The release keeps its assets.
  • The image of secureblue-images installs chora from COPR.
  • The session starts through uwsm (D50). A flavor is a systemd target.
  • The tiling flavor: chora-tiling with waybar, fuzzel, mako, swaylock, swayidle and kanshi (D51).
  • Input device settings through the API: tap, acceleration, natural scroll, key repeat. A view sets them, so the core reads no file (D35).
  • Output hotplug, suspend and resume, lid switch, and the VT switch on the reference hardware.
  • Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr, and X11 apps through xwayland-satellite.

Gate:

  1. The secureblue image builds with chora from COPR. rpm-ostree upgrade on the reference hardware updates chora, and the login screen offers the session.
  2. The user works 10 working days in a row only in chora on the reference hardware. coredumpctl list chora shows no entry, and the log shows no emergency reset that the user did not start.
  3. A checklist on the reference hardware passes, with the log of each step. An external monitor goes in and out 10 times, and the laptop suspends and resumes 10 times. The user closes and opens the lid, switches the VT, and locks and unlocks the session. A screen share in a browser and an X11 app work.
  4. The vkms job covers hotplug of a second output.
  5. The AUR packages build in CI.
  6. A view sets tap and key repeat, and a test shows that the core applies them.
  7. The gate checks of the earlier milestones still hold, and the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: 1.0: Stable API
docs.text:
Goal: the API is version 1 and stays compatible until 2.0.

Scope:

  • The protocol version 1: a JSON schema of all methods, events and errors in the repository, generated from chora-scene. A CI job fails on a change of the schema without a change of the protocol version.
  • The reference documentation comes from the schema. A test checks every example of the documentation against it.
  • A final review loop over the whole code base until a round finds nothing that matters (D47).
  • All plugins of the organization use the protocol version 1.

Gate:

  1. The user works 30 days with the release candidate as the daily session. coredumpctl list chora shows no entry.
  2. No open issue has the label severity:high.
  3. The last review round leaves no open finding of high or medium severity.
  4. The schema job and the documentation test are green.
  5. Every plugin repository of the organization pins protocol version 1, and a CI job checks it.
  6. The gate checks of the earlier milestones still hold, and the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.

docs.title: Track: XP showroom
docs.text:
The showroom moves to chora/chora-xp in milestone 0.6 and grows in parallel (D39). It shows the effects of the scene and serves as their test.

  • Each core milestone ends with a showroom release that uses its API. The core gate checks that the showroom CI is green against the release candidate.
  • Scope and order of new effects are the decision of the user. Each new effect gets a pixel test in tests/xp.sh.

docs.title: Track: voice pipeline
docs.text:
The voice pipeline lives in chora/chora-voice and starts with milestone 0.6 (D53). It runs as Quadlet units on the reference hardware: speech to text, a router model, a main model and text to speech, served by Gufo.

Milestone Goal Gate Needs from the core V1 Pipeline speech in, an answer as speech out, with barge-in median 1.0 s or less from the end of speech to the first audio, over 20 German utterances nothing V2 Control the voice agent drives chora through MCP "move the terminal to the right" works in 18 of 20 tries 0.7 (push-to-talk with input.grab-any), 0.8 (read model, text injection) V3 Views a morning view and task views "show my tasks for today" opens a view with the tasks of an MCP source; "open a view for the first task" opens a view with two surfaces 0.8

docs.title: After 1.0
docs.text:
• Conformance tests with wlcs.
  • Items from the Idea backlog.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Three scenarios test the concept and estimate the effort on top of the core. The estimates are rough. They assume that the core implements the common Wayland protocols (see Dependencies), so existing tools work unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Classic desktop
docs.text:
A Windows-like desktop with taskbar, start menu and overlapping windows, driven by mouse and keyboard. This is not the goal of chora, but it must be possible.

Part Source Effort Stacking window manager: move, resize, raise, focus, minimize plugin about 1000 to 2000 lines Window decorations: title bar, buttons plugin with rect and shader nodes, a decoration surface of the plugin, or client-side decorations small to medium Keybindings: Alt+Tab, Super key plugin small Taskbar, tray, clock existing shell: Quickshell, waybar, eww configuration Start menu, launcher fuzzel, wofi or a Quickshell widget configuration Wallpaper swaybg or swww configuration Pixel-perfect XP look theme assets, shaders, decorations much detail work, little difficulty

The taskbar needs the foreign-toplevel protocols to see the windows. The launcher and the bar need wlr-layer-shell.

Result: medium effort, almost all of it in one window manager plugin.

docs.title: 2. Keyboard-driven tiling
docs.text:
A Linux-style tiling workflow with workspaces. The user configures it.

Part Source Effort Tiling layout: master and stack, columns, scrolling plugin a few hundred lines Workspaces one group per workspace, switched by visibility or transform small Keybindings, focus movement plugin small Bar waybar or Quickshell configuration Animations the animate command of the core small

Result: low effort. This is a good first flavor to test the plugin API.

docs.title: 3. Agentic workday
docs.text:
This scenario is the core idea. A robust voice channel connects the user to an agent, and the agent arranges content for each task.

  1. Morning view. The agent greets the user and shows the current tasks. It sorts the email. User and agent plan and prioritize the day together.
  2. Task views. The agent builds a new canvas for each task and fills it. A data analysis gets prepared data, plots and interactive exploration. Email, web research and coding get their own views.
  3. Reuse. The inventory keeps useful elements in git for later use. The agent discards code for one-time use.
  4. Live change by voice. "Make the plot bigger." "Put the terminal next to the notebook." "Dim everything except the editor." The agent calls the methods of the window manager plugin for these changes.
Part Source Effort Scene access for the agent IPC socket and choractl mcp part of the API Speech in and out the voice pipeline of chora-voice (D53) integration The agent Claude Code or another MCP client, later a local LLM service integration Rich content: greeting, plots, email the agent writes HTML, a browser in app mode shows it as a surface generated content Data exploration Jupyter, marimo or a plot web app as surfaces existing tools One view per task YAML views that choractl loads, saves and changes live coordinator tool Inventory, memory opinionated layer above chora later

Result: the largest scenario, but mostly integration of existing parts. The core must supply scene queries and changes, screenshots and input injection. The agent needs screenshots to see the result of its changes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
• The five node kinds cover all three scenarios.
  • Widgets and rich content do not need to live in the core. Existing shells, wallpaper tools and a browser in app mode supply them. Short labels come from the text node of milestone 0.8 (D18).
  • Two core features decide the success. The protocol coverage lets existing tools work. The API lets plugins and agents arrange everything.

docs.title: Vision and principles
docs.text: chora is the space where forms appear.

docs.title: The name
docs.text: Plato calls the space in which things come into being chora (χώρα). chora is neither form nor matter. It only gives the forms a place. The compositor works the same way: it has no content and no policy of its own. Plugins, clients and agents bring the forms.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A desktop decides the arrangement of the content: windows, panels, workspaces. chora takes this decision out of the compositor. chora is a programmable scene. It works more like a game engine than like a window manager. The core renders a scene of nodes. One API changes the scene live.

The motivating use case is agentic interaction. The user talks to an agent, ideally by voice. The agent arranges the screen for the current task and for the taste of the user. Examples are a morning view, a data exploration view and a coding view. The agent changes the arrangement while the user works.

Agents are the motivation, not a requirement. The same scene can host a pixel-perfect Windows XP desktop, a keyboard-driven tiling setup or a KDE-like workflow. It can also host a kind of human-machine interaction that does not exist yet. chora ships none of them. chora makes all of them possible.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Everything is a plugin. The core has no policy: no layout, no focus model, no keybindings, no decorations, no defaults. The window manager is a plugin too. A core without plugins shows a black screen.
  2. Safety is the only built-in behavior. The core keeps an escape hatch that no plugin can override: VT switch, quit, and an emergency reset. Agents will write broken code live, so this exception is necessary.
  3. Lean core, checked stability. The core stays small. Features grow in plugins, not in the core. A milestone is done only when its gate holds (D46).
  4. Reuse before writing. Wayland protocol handling, rendering, widgets, shells and services already exist. chora connects these parts and writes only what is missing. Fixes go upstream. Every decision gets a check for existing alternatives.
  5. One API for every caller. Plugins, scripts, the CLI, services and agents use the same scene language. An agent can change everything that a user can configure, and it can change it live.
  6. Live and real time. Changes apply while the session runs. They need no restart and cause no noticeable latency.
  7. Declarative and versioned. The configuration is plain text in git: views in YAML, and flavors as bundles of files. A diff shows each change. An agent can read and write the files easily.
  8. Isolation by default. Plugins run as separate processes, services in containers. Input injection and screen capture through the API need a capability that the user gives (D33).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Reach 1.0: a daily driver on the reference hardware with a stable, versioned API (D3).
  • Run as an additional session on a Fedora host, next to the existing desktops. The concrete host is a derived secureblue image.
  • Add features as plugins and as services in containers.
  • Let a coordinator install and connect plugins and services. The first coordinator is the user. A later coordinator is an agent with special permissions that can also write new plugins and services.
  • Make it possible to rebuild any existing workflow, with effort, and to invent new ones.

docs.title: Non-goals before 1.0
docs.text:
• A usable desktop out of the box. A flavor can supply one. The core never does.
  • Agent memory and a local inventory of reusable elements. These form a separate, opinionated layer on top of chora (see Idea backlog).
  • Distributions other than Fedora, secureblue and Arch Linux, and NVIDIA GPUs (D11).
